newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Egypt investments to boost confidence in Mideast.
newsitem.headline: Egypt investments to boost confidence in Mideast.

text.p: Egyptian Prime Minister Kamal Ganzouri said on Thursday business investments in his country serve as a vote of confidence for the Middle East peace process.
He was winding up a three-day trade promotion and investment mission to Singapore that brought a flurry of agreements.
Singapore and Egypt signed three memorandum of understanding (MOU) agreements for trade, shipping and overall investment.
These followed the signing earlier of agreements on investment guarantees and avoidance of double taxation.
"If we go ahead and have more and more economic cooperation in the area, this will be action for peace," Ganzouri said.
He said Singapore and Malaysia, which Ganzouri visited earlier in the week, had both expressed support for the Middle East peace process.
"They believe that peace is very important, very valuable and that we must reach it. Some colleagues are afraid there will be some problems there," Ganzouri said.
But he said he was confident peace would prevail, especially if Egypt and others invested in the region to give further assurance of stability.
Thursday's MOU on economic, trade and investment cooperation was signed by Ganzouri and Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong, and is expected to boost technology investment.
The framework for Thursday's MOU rests on both countries encouraging their private sectors to establish joint ventures, and cooperate on technical matters and international issues.
A member of the Egyptian delegation told Reuters the aim of the present government was to attract about US$10 billion a year in investment for Egypt.
Singapore's Trade and Development Board plans to send a mission to Egypt in the third quarter this year and in 1998.
The Port of Singapore Authority will participate in Egypt's port development and construction of container service.

Singapore's trade with Egypt has been increasing at an average annual rate of 11 percent since 1988. But in 1996 trade declined, totalling S$332.7 million (US231 million), a 13.8 percent fall from 1995's $386 million.
